newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy appoints "undertaker" for IRI.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy appoints "undertaker" for IRI.

text.p: Italy on Sunday named a new chairman and board for indebted state industrial holding IRI to oversee the privatisation of sellable assets and wind up the ailing giant's operations.

A Treasury statement said the new appointments, which would see outgoing chairman Michele Tedeschi replaced by Gian Maria Gros-Pietro, would be put to an IRI shareholders' meeting on Monday. The Treasury is sole shareholder.

The widely-expected move came after Tedeschi, chairman since 1994 and with 25 years service within IRI (Istituto per la Ricostruzione Industriale), publicly rejected growing criticism of being lukewarm on the privatisation front.

Political sources said the Treasury made the announcement before Monday's meeting because both Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi are attending the European Union summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday.

"The mandate that we intend to give the new board is to carry forward the privatisations and liquidations of companies which come under IRI with a commitment to conclude the process and proceed to the cessation of the institute's activities within three years," the statement said.
It thanked Tedeschi for what the Treasury called the dedication and expertise "with which he has led the institute in its difficult phase of transition".

Gros-Pietro, an economist, is currently a board member of ANAS, the national road maintenance company, and since 1994 has been a member of the Treasury's privatisation committee. He is also a close acquaintance of Prodi, a former IRI chairman.

IRI, set up by fascist dictator Benito Mussolini in 1933 to rescue the Italian banking industry, had a gross debt mountain of 23.5 trillion lire ($14 billion) in late 1996. Government eagerness for a quick sell-off of assets has led to tensions with the outgoing board.

Prodi was twice chairman of IRI, from 1982-89 and from 1993-94, before resigning to be replaced by Tedeschi. Prodi then entered the political arena culminating in his victory in April 1996 elections at the head of a centre-left government.
The largest industrial group in the country, the sprawling giant controls through holding companies hundreds of businesses in sectors as diverse as broadcasting and shipbuilding.

Italian newspapers have reported that Treasury plans foresee IRI not being assigned new tasks but concentrating of privatising existing assets, initially motorway operator Autostrade and Rome airports both set for this year.
Other assets owned by IRI include engineering group Finmeccanica, shipbuilder Fincantieri and state airline Alitalia.
Finmeccanica recently saw a radical shake up of top management over differences of opinion on the method and speed of the privatisation programme.

The privatisation of state-controlled telecommunications company Telecom Italia due in October following its merger with former IRI holding Stet is a key part of government efforts to reduce IRI's debt mountain to a level agreed with the European Union's executive Commission.
The government decided last year to transfer IRI's stake in Stet to the Treasury and to pay IRI some 14 trillion lire.
In order to raise capital both for IRI and the Treasury, several of the group's companies have already been sold.
In 1993 the group privatized its Credito Italiano and Banca Commerciale Italiana banks and its SME food business. In 1996, IRI sold off its remaining ILVA steel interests.
